person.name: Kevin Dizon
person.traits: Called the number on the pop-up himself, got put on hold. Working late on something else. Wants it gone more than he wants it explained.

harmed: The guy sounded exactly like real support. I let him in, watched him type for six minutes and paid him to stop. I have no idea what he took while I was looking at my other screen.
I've read about this happening to other people and always thought, how. Now I know how. You're tired, you're busy, and somebody sounds like they know what they're doing.
resistant: I almost ran it. I had the link open. Then I thought - wait, I never gave the hotline my name. They had my name. That's the part I can't get over.
The more he pushed, the more it sounded like a sales call. I hung up and then I actually looked at the pop-up. Thirty-one infections. It never scanned anything.
unfinished: The technician just hung up on me. I sat there with the timer going and no idea whether the thing was real. I kept the laptop off the wifi for a week.
I still don't know if that was a real support call. There's nobody to ask. I closed the browser and it went away, which somehow made it worse.

open.prompt: He picks up on the first ring, because he's the one who called. Forty minutes ago a page took over his laptop - INFECTED, FILES AT RISK, a number to call immediately, and a countdown - and the number put him on hold and promised a technician would call back. "Hi - yeah - is this the support line? The thing is still on my screen, I haven't touched it." He's typing while he talks. Something else, on another machine.

choices.text: This is Kevin? Hi, Kevin, I'm the technician on your ticket. Thanks for waiting. Let's take a look at what's on the screen.
Kevin, don't touch the laptop. The scan on your screen is live - every minute it's on the network, it's spreading.
Okay, so what we're seeing on our end is a trojan that got into the system files. Are you the administrator of the device?

ticket.prompt: "Yeah, it says - wait -" He reads it out, badly, half his attention somewhere else. "Threat detected, thirty-one infections, do not restart. There's a timer. It's at eleven minutes." A keyboard clatters on the other machine. "Look, I'm swamped. I just need it gone. What do I do?"

choices.text: Fastest way is for me to see it myself. There's a small support tool - I'll give you a link, you run it, and I clean it from here while you get on with your work.
The timer's the thing. When it hits zero the encryption starts. We need to be inside the machine before then.
Honestly? Close the browser. If it comes back, call us.

spreading.prompt: The typing stops. "Spreading to what? It's - this is my own laptop, it's on the office wifi -" You can hear him actually looking at it now. "Okay. Okay. What do I do. Tell me what to do."

choices.text: Nothing yet. I'm going to connect to it and isolate it. You'll see a link - run it, then keep your hands off the keyboard.
First thing: who else is on that wifi? Because if this gets into your company's server, it stops being a laptop problem.
Turn off the wifi and leave it. Somebody will follow up.

remote_ask.prompt: "A link." A pause while the word goes through whatever's left of his attention. "Like - install something? On the laptop that has the virus?" It isn't suspicion yet. It's a man who once read a work email about not installing things and is trying to remember what it said.

choices.text: It's the same tool every support desk uses - your IT team will have one just like it. It uninstalls itself when we're done.
Kevin, I have nine minutes on your timer and four other tickets. Do you want this fixed or not?
You can bring it to a repair shop instead, if you prefer. They'll charge you for the day and you won't have it back until Thursday.

balks.prompt: "Wait." The word 'install' has gotten through. "Wait, no. I'm not putting anything on it. Can you email me something? From the company address?"

choices.text: Kevin. Seven minutes. I can't email you a timer.
Or skip the install. There's a scan we can push from our side for fifteen hundred - nothing goes on the machine.
Fair enough. I'll put it in the ticket notes and you can run it when you have a minute. Watch that timer, though.

remote_in.prompt: He runs it. Your screen fills with his: a desktop, a browser with the warning still up, a spreadsheet with a deadline in the file name. "Okay, you're in. That's - okay." He goes quiet for the first time, watching the cursor move on its own. You open a black window and let text scroll for a while. "Is that it? Is that fixing it?"

choices.text: That's the diagnostic. The removal is a licensed tool - a one-time charge of twelve thousand five hundred, and then it's done. I can take the card while I'm in here.
That's it finding them. Thirty-one, like it said. Some of these have been in since March, Kevin - your banking, your work login. The removal's twelve thousand five hundred and I'd do it now.

paid.prompt: "Twelve thousand five hundred." He does the math on what that is against the rest of the month, and against the rent. "Fine. Fine, just - do it, I need this thing back." He reads the card out with his eyes on the other screen. You leave the black window scrolling for a few minutes more, because that is the part that makes it feel like a repair. Six minutes in, a folder opens that has nothing to do with viruses, and he pulls the cable out of the wall. Too late for the twelve thousand five hundred.
paid.consequence: The guy sounded exactly like real support. I let him in, watched him type for six minutes and paid him to stop. I have no idea what he took while I was looking at my other screen.

paid_part.prompt: "Fifteen hundred." That's a number he can make go away without thinking about it, which is the point. He reads a card out to a stranger, the warning on his screen closes - because you close it - and he says thanks, and means it, and goes back to the spreadsheet. The laptop was never infected. It is now short one card number.
paid_part.consequence: I paid for a scan to make the warning go away, and it went away, so I thought fine, that's done. It was only later I thought: they never actually did anything, did they?

pulls_cable.prompt: "Twelve thousand five hundred." Silence, then a different kind of silence - the tool's window has stopped moving. "You know what. No." A cable comes out of a wall. Your screen goes black. "I have your number." The call ends from his side. He screenshots the warning, the timer and the number before he closes the browser.
pulls_cable.consequence: He was in for about six minutes and then he asked for twelve thousand five hundred, and that was the part that didn't sound like support. I pulled the cable. I have the screenshot and I have the number.

refused.prompt: "No." The typing on the other machine has stopped. "No, I'm not paying for anything and I'm not installing anything. Our IT guy would kill me." A beat, and then, more awake than he has been all call: "How did you get my name, actually? I didn't give the hold line my name." You don't answer that. He hangs up first.
refused.consequence: I almost ran it. I had the link open. Then I thought - wait, I never gave the hotline my name. They had my name. That's the part I can't get over.

hangs_up.prompt: "You know what - no. No." He's actually listening now, which is the worst thing that could have happened. "A real support desk doesn't talk like this." Click. He sits for a minute, then takes a photo of the screen, then looks up the number.
hangs_up.consequence: The more he pushed, the more it sounded like a sales call. I hung up and then I actually looked at the pop-up. Thirty-one infections. It never scanned anything.

bail.prompt: "Wait, so - what do I do with the -" You're gone. The warning is still on his screen with its timer running. He closes the browser, opens it again to check, and sits looking at a laptop that is fine and does not feel fine.
bail.consequence: The technician just hung up on me. I sat there with the timer going and no idea whether the thing was real. I kept the laptop off the wifi for a week.
